blocks.text: Meet Claude

Before any prompt or trick, the thing that decides whether Claude works for you is something quieter: what you expect from it. Claude isn't a faster chatbot — it's a reasoning partner that rewards a clear frame and goes vague when you don't give it one. And once you get it, everything else becomes easier — throughout this course, we'll take a closer look at how it's done.
First Impressions Matter

If you're coming to Claude from another AI tool, it might feel a little different at first. The answers may seem cautious, and the creativity might feel restrained. Sometimes Claude asks clarifying questions instead of jumping in.

That difference reflects a different design philosophy.
How Claude Approaches Problems
Instead of guessing, Claude reasons carefully before responding. It tries to:

• Collect context
  • Understand intent
  • Consider implications
  • Avoid oversimplified conclusions
This makes Claude especially strong at tasks where clarity, nuance, and structure matter more than speed. It serves as your thinking partner instead of just generating answers.
Claude performs especially well when you need to:

• Work through complex ideas
  • Analyze long or detailed material
  • Refine writing or arguments
  • Explore sensitive or ambiguous topics
In these situations, Claude's careful approach becomes a real advantage. It serves as your thinking partner instead of just generating answers.
Where Claude Struggles
That same careful design can make Claude struggle when:

• The task goal is vague
  • The prompt relies on guesswork
  • You ask it to create something but don't set boundaries
  • Speed matters more than depth
When this happens, Claude is waiting for clearer direction.

blocks.text: Claude's Models
Claude's performance and output quality depend on the model you go with. The tool offers a range of models:

• Haiku — fast and light for simple tasks
  • Sonnet — the balanced everyday choice
  • Opus — powerful for advanced reasoning and complex projects
  • Fable — designed for highly complex tasks, research, and long-running workflows

Available models depend on your plan. Free users typically get Haiku and Sonnet, while paid plans unlock Opus and Fable. Fable is a premium model with separate usage limits and may require additional credits. Note: Model availability, usage limits, and access requirements may change over time. Check Claude for the latest options available on your account.
One More Dial: Effort

Next to the model name sits an effort control: turn it up, and Claude thinks longer and more thoroughly before answering; turn it down for faster replies. But neither dial fixes a vague prompt — more effort just gets you a thorough answer to the wrong question. The model and effort change how hard Claude works; your frame still decides what it works on.
Claude vs. Other AI Tools

So how does Claude itself compare to the other tools you might already reach for? If you've used tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, or DeepSeek, Claude may feel familiar at first — but the differences show up quickly as tasks become more complex.

These AIs aren't better or worse overall. They're optimized for different kinds of thinking and different working styles.
Claude and ChatGPT: Different Priorities

ChatGPT is optimized for speed, flexibility, and conversational flow. It often jumps into a task quickly, even when the goal is loosely defined.

Claude takes a more deliberate approach. It prefers clarity before action and tends to reason through implications before producing an answer.
If you ask both tools: "Help me write a welcome email for new customers."

• ChatGPT will likely jump straight into a draft — friendly, upbeat, ready to send. Fast and useful if you just need something now.
  • Claude is more likely to pause and ask: "What kind of customers? What tone fits your brand? Is there a specific action you want them to take?" It wants to understand before it writes.
Claude and Gemini: Focus vs. Breadth

Gemini is designed to work across a wide range of tasks and environments, especially Google's ecosystem. It adapts quickly and shines in tasks involving integrations, tools, or rapid synthesis.

Claude focuses more narrowly on reasoning quality and language consistency. It strongly maintains coherence across long conversations or large documents.
If you paste a 20-page contract and ask: "What should I watch out for?"

• Gemini might scan quickly, pull key terms, and give you a broad summary with links to relevant resources. Efficient and wide-ranging.
  • Claude is more likely to walk through the document section by section, flag specific clauses that could create risk, and explain why each one matters in plain language.
Claude and DeepSeek: Caution vs. Speed

DeepSeek is optimized for efficiency and rapid problem-solving. It tends to move quickly from prompt to output, often producing confident answers even with minimal instructions.

Claude takes a more cautious path. It prioritizes understanding the full context before responding and is more likely to slow down, clarify, or hedge when information is incomplete.
Imagine you ask both tools: "What are the risks of expanding into a new market?"

• DeepSeek will likely give you a quick, confident list — market saturation, regulatory hurdles, currency risk — and move on. Efficient and to the point.
  • Claude is more likely to ask what kind of market you're in, which industry, and what your current position looks like before answering. Then it'll walk through each risk with context specific to your situation.

When tasks are simple, the differences between models can feel minor. As complexity increases, patterns emerge:
  • Claude asks clarifying questions more often
  • Claude avoids guessing
  • Claude maintains tone and logic over long responses
This can feel slower at first — but it often reduces rewrites, corrections, and misunderstandings later.

blocks.text: From Conversations to Workflows
Now that you know how Claude approaches problems, it's time to see what it can actually build. Next up, you'll get hands-on with:

• Projects — workspaces within Claude that keep your context, instructions, and files organized across conversations.

In the next lesson, you'll start with Projects — a way to keep context and goals consistent across longer work. Ready to uncover Claude's full potential?
Working With Projects
Have you ever started a new chat to continue working on something, only to realize that AI doesn't remember what you discussed before?
You end up re-explaining your goals, repeating constraints, and rebuilding context from scratch. The more complex the task, the more frustrating this gets.
Claude's Projects is a feature designed to solve exactly this. Let's see how it works!
Scenario: Planning a Renovation
Imagine you're planning a home renovation. You want to:

• Estimate a rough budget
  • Think through the order of work
  • Compare materials
  • Revisit decisions as new constraints appear
You open Claude and start asking questions.

blocks.text: Feeling the Friction

You ask about flooring, then about plumbing and lighting.

Each answer is helpful on its own — but none of them "remember" the bigger picture you're building. Earlier constraints fade unless you restate them.

The problem isn't Claude's reasoning. It's the lack of a stable frame.
A Different Approach

This is where Projects come in. It is a dedicated workspace where you set up your context once, and Claude carries it across every conversation inside it. To create a project, go to Projects → New Project, give it a name and a short description of what it's for.
Then, there are two spaces to fill:

1. Instructions: your goals, constraints, and preferences in plain language.
  2. Files, where you can attach any documents related to your work.

On higher-tier plans, a Project also has a "Memory" block, where Claude can hold onto details it learns as you work — and that Memory stays scoped to just this Project. If you don't see it, don't worry: your instructions and files already carry the context that matters most.

As a result, every time you start a new chat inside the Project, Claude will automatically see those instructions and files. You don't paste them again — they're just there.

It's like giving Claude a briefing before every conversation, without actually having to brief it every time.
In the context of renovation planning, this approach will make Claude keep and always see:

• The overall goal
  • Previous decisions
  • Constraints you've already discussed
Setting Up a Project
To set up a Project, start by describing context in the "Instructions" block. For example:

• The size of the apartment
  • Your rough budget range
  • The rooms involved
  • What matters most (cost, speed, quality, or style)
It will become the foundation that everything else builds on.
In addition, you can also break the plan into phases and instruct Claude on:

• What should happen first
  • Which steps depend on others
  • Where decisions can wait
This will help Claude memorize the overall plan and respond effectively in every chat inside the Project.

To make this clearer, imagine you want to discuss flooring and lighting separately without mixing everything into one long chat. 

With a Project set up, you can simply open a new chat inside it for each phase:

• One for flooring
  • Another for lighting
  • A third one for plumbing
Each chat stays focused, but Claude will still know your overall budget, priorities, and earlier decisions.
This gives you two things at once:

1. You're no longer re-explaining your full situation every time you ask a question — Claude already has the context.
  2. You keep everything organized, with each phase in its own conversation instead of buried in one endless thread.
Revising Without Resetting

Now, imagine that a week later, you get new contractor quotes — the budget changes. Does it mean that you should start it all over again? Before Projects, this would've indeed been an issue. But with this feature, not at all!

• Planning that requires revisiting assumptions

  • Learning complex topics over time
  • Comparing options and tradeoffs repeatedly
In these cases, continuity isn't just convenient — it actively improves the quality of thinking.

Claude's Creative Potential

In Unit 1, you learned what Claude is and the spaces you build in. Now we shift to something more powerful: how you ask. Today we explore techniques that encourage more creative and innovative responses from Claude — and the surprise is that the right frame doesn't limit Claude's imagination, it directs it. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to craft prompts that inspire Claude to generate original, imaginative, and unconventional ideas.

Creative prompting means using specific techniques to encourage Claude to generate more original, imaginative, and unconventional responses.

Counterintuitively, creativity in Claude often comes from limits — a clear frame is what gives imagination something to push against.
Frame 1: Constraints

The clearest way to see this is with constraints. It sounds backwards — shouldn't limits kill creativity? 

But when you cap the budget, the time, the format, or the audience, you push Claude off the obvious path and force it to invent.

Suppose you're brainstorming an app with Artifacts that helps with budgeting. A simple "Design a budgeting app for people who find money stressful" prompt gave you this. Let's see how to get more interesting solutions from Claude here.

blocks.text: Imposing Arbitrary Constraints

By imposing arbitrary constraints — like limiting resources or time — you force Claude to think creatively within strict boundaries. This can lead to more inventive solutions, as constraints often inspire out-of-the-box problem-solving.

blocks.exampleResponse:
A pop-up exhibition booth built from five materials in one week:
  1. Aluminum frame modules — lightweight, reusable structure
  2. Fabric wall panels — flexible surfaces for visuals and branding
  3. LED strip lighting — integrated illumination with low setup time
  4. Modular flooring tiles — quick assembly without tools
  5. Magnetic fasteners — tool-free connections
The booth is designed for rapid deployment and teardown. All components fit into standardized cases, allowing transport and assembly by a small team. The layout adapts to different spaces without redesign.
blocks.prompt: Сreate a prompt that imposes arbitrary constraints to inspire creative problem-solving.
blocks.template: Design [everyday object] that can be built with only [number] materials and [timeframe]

blocks.text: By limiting Claude, you push it to think creatively, finding unique solutions under these constraints. If you ask "give me ideas for a coffee shop" — you get generic and random instead of useful. Add one twist: "design a coffee shop for people who hate coffee." Suddenly Claude has to invent — tea flights, a dessert-and-conversation bar. Same topic; one frame that forces originality.
blocks.title: What a Constraint Does

blocks.text: Frame 2: Posing Unusual Situations

Constraints are just one kind of creative frame. You can inspire Claude another way: pose an impossible or unusual situation, and Claude has to reason its way through it. 

"What if" questions and strange hypotheticals give imagination a runway — a frame built from a premise that doesn't exist yet.

blocks.exampleResponse:
In a world with hourly gravitational shifts, transportation and architecture would face unprecedented challenges. Vehicles would need omnidirectional propulsion systems as roads become temporarily vertical or inverted. Buildings would require 360° structural integrity with no true "roof" or "floor." Three innovative solutions:
  1. Spherical Architecture: Buildings designed as reinforced geodesic spheres with modular interiors that automatically reorient furniture and fixtures with each gravity shift.
  2. Magnetic Anchor Systems: Personal and vehicle-based electromagnetic tethering technology allowing controlled movement regardless of gravitational direction.
  3. Predictive AI Navigation: Algorithms forecasting gravity shifts to automatically reroute transportation and trigger building system adaptations before changes occur.
blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt that encourages creative thinking.
blocks.template: [Command] a world where gravity [unusual scenario] every hour. Describe how this would affect [aspect of life] and propose [number] innovative solutions to overcome potential challenges.

blocks.text: Great! This technique sets up an unusual scenario and prompts Claude to think creatively. Bringing up something unexpected always makes Claude move past conventional responses.
Frame 3: Combining Unrelated Concepts
Mix two ideas from different worlds, and Claude builds something neither would produce alone. Describe an everyday object as something it's not, and a new function emerges from the collision.

blocks.exampleResponse:
Imagine your smartphone as a sentient companion — a warm, responsive being with glass skin and digital veins. It breathes in data, learns your habits, and anticipates your needs through empathic connection rather than algorithms.

This living phone might physically adapt to circumstances — stretching for better viewing, curling around your wrist when needed, or generating warmth when you're cold. It could heal minor scratches, regulate its own energy needs, and express emotions through subtle color changes and vibrations.

Most significantly, it might prioritize your well-being over task efficiency, suggesting breaks during extended use or connecting you with loved ones when sensing your loneliness.
blocks.prompt: Now, fill in the gaps to create a prompt using one of these techniques.
blocks.template: Describe [everyday object] as if it were [unrelated concept]. How might its function change, and what new uses could it have in this form?

blocks.text: See how that worked? Fusing a smartphone with a living being pushed Claude toward functions a plain "improve my phone" prompt never would — healing, adapting, sensing. Two inputs, one new thing.
Frame 4: Reversing Assumptions

This technique also challenges conventional ideas or expectations. But instead of fusing two ideas into something new, you take a single assumption everyone accepts — and flip it. "What if a library were loud?" "What if customers paid less the more they bought?" Inverting one default forces fresh thinking from a single idea, not two.

Enhancing Claude's Analysis

In the last lesson, creative frames opened possibilities up. Analytical frameworks do the opposite job: they give Claude a fixed structure to think within, turning a sprawling question into focused, organized analysis. Same core skill you've been building — handing Claude a lens — pointed now at rigor instead of range.
Claude Thinks in Frameworks

When you ask Claude an open-ended question, it can organize its thinking through analytical frameworks. This turns a vague answer into a focused, structured one.

And while the examples here are business-focused, the same approach works for anything complex: career decisions, policy questions, creative projects, research.
The Skill Is Choosing the Lens

Running a framework is the easy part — Claude does that on request. The real skill is picking the right one for your question. 

A framework built for internal strengths won't tell you about market pressure, and one built for competition won't sort your product line. Match the lens to what you actually need to see.

blocks.text: Combining Two Frameworks

One framework gives you one angle. But what if you're building a product strategy and need to understand both what your company is good at and what the market looks like? That's when combining two frameworks in one prompt becomes powerful.
Here are two frameworks worth knowing before you try it:

• VRIO (Value, Rarity, Imitability, Organization) breaks down what a company has going for it internally and whether those advantages are actually hard for competitors to copy.
  • Porter's Five Forces maps five sources of pressure that shape how competitive an industry is: new players entering, supplier influence, buyer power, substitute products, and rivalry between existing competitors.
Together, they cover what neither can alone: internal capability and external competition.

blocks.exampleResponse: VRIO Framework (Internal) - Valuable: Solves real customer pain points - Rare: Unique workflow integrations - Inimitable: Proprietary data insights - Organized: Teams structured to scale innovation Porter's Five Forces (External) - New Entrants: Moderate barriers due to switching costs - Supplier Power: Low (multiple infrastructure providers) - Buyer Power: Medium (price sensitivity varies) - Substitutes: Alternative tools exist but lack depth - Rivalry: Competitive but fragmented market This combination reveals both internal strengths and external pressures shaping strategy.

Complex Webs of Knowledge

Across this unit, you've been shaping how Claude thinks — opening possibilities with creative frames, then structuring analysis with frameworks. Both focus Claude on one subject at a time. 

This final technique goes wider: real problems rarely stay in one lane, so you'll learn to have Claude trace how things connect — across different fields, through a whole system, and over time.
Cross-Domain Analysis

Imagine you're curious about how artificial intelligence is changing the world. You could ask Claude about AI in healthcare. Or AI in education. Or AI in manufacturing. Each answer would be useful on its own. But what if you asked Claude to look at all three at once — and compare how the same technology plays out differently in each field? That's cross-domain analysis.
This approach pushes Claude to analyze one idea across multiple areas side by side. When it does, it often reveals connections and contrasts that you'd miss by looking at each field separately.

blocks.exampleResponse:
The widespread adoption of AI will transform healthcare, education, and manufacturing in distinct ways. In healthcare, AI enhances diagnostics, personalizes treatment, and optimizes patient care. Education benefits from AI-driven personalized learning, virtual tutors, and automated grading, improving access and efficiency. Both sectors prioritize human-AI collaboration to enhance service quality and outcomes.

In contrast, manufacturing focuses on efficiency and cost reduction through automation. AI enables predictive maintenance, smart production lines, and optimized supply chains, significantly boosting productivity. Ethical concerns like data privacy in healthcare and bias in education differ from job displacement fears in manufacturing, highlighting varied societal impacts across these sectors.

Let's move on!
Systems Thinking Approach

Now, suppose you want to look at a company's work processes overall instead of looking at separate fields. Product development, marketing, and customer support aren't independent — they're all connected, and you want to explore these interactions. That's where systems thinking comes in. Instead of analyzing areas separately, it focuses on how different parts of a system interact and influence each other.

Again, consider a company as a system. A change in one area — like accelerating product releases — can affect support workload and marketing timelines.

Systems thinking helps reveal these interdependencies.

blocks.exampleResponse: From a systems thinking perspective, the global supply chain includes production, logistics, inventory management, and customer demand. Changes in demand influence production schedules, which affect logistics capacity and inventory levels. Feedback loops emerge when delays or shortages shift customer expectations, further impacting demand patterns.

The Causal Chain: Tracing Effects Over Time

Causal relationships explore how changes in one area can cause effects in another. A change never stops at its first effect — it sets off a chain: the immediate result, then the ripples that spread outward, then the indirect consequences that only surface later. Most answers stop at the first link. The skill is teaching Claude to follow the whole chain.
Layer 1: The First-Order Effect

Start with direct cause and effect: a change in one place produces an immediate result. 

How does a pricing change in a subscription service affect customer retention? That's the first link — visible and expected. Naming it clearly gives Claude a solid base to build the rest of the chain on.

The deepest layer: the indirect effects that show up after the dust settles. 

Automating routine tasks speeds things up at first — but then skill requirements shift, training needs change, and eventually the whole team structure evolves. These second-order effects are the ones most people miss, and they're often what matters most.

Writing & Editing With Claude

Welcome to Unit 3, where everything you've learned about shaping Claude's thinking goes to work on real tasks — starting with the one you do most: writing. You've finished something that matters — a proposal, a report, an email. And that's where the real work happens: not the first draft, but the editing after. Claude's strength here is working as an editorial partner that improves what you wrote without erasing your voice.
The Difference Shows Up in Revision

Imagine you've drafted an internal memo about upcoming team changes. You know what you want to say, but reading it back, it feels scattered. Some parts sound too casual, others feel stiff.

You could spend an hour rewriting it yourself. Or you could hand it to Claude — not to replace what you wrote but to refine it.

feedbackCorrect.text: When you've been working on something, your brain assumes that readers will understand everything easily. You see what you meant to say, not what's actually on the page.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The problem isn't memory or skill — it's perspective. You need distance from your own work to see where it breaks down for someone reading it fresh.

options.label: You're too close to the work to see where it's unclear
You lack the technical skill to improve it

blocks.text: Scenario: Revising a Team Memo

Here's your draft: "Team, some changes are coming up. Starting next month, Sarah's moving into the product lead role, which means her current responsibilities will shift to Marcus and Jen. We're also bringing on two new hires to support the launch, and they'll report directly to me for now. The project timeline isn't changing, but the way we're structuring work is going to look different. Let me know if you have questions." The information is there. But the structure is loose. "Some changes" is vague. "Work is going to look different" doesn't tell people what to expect.

blocks.exampleResponse:
Team, I want to share some upcoming organizational changes that will take effect next month.

Sarah is moving into the product lead role. Her current project coordination responsibilities will transfer to Marcus, and Jen will take over stakeholder communication.

We're also bringing on two new hires to support the launch. They'll report directly to me during onboarding, and we'll reassess the reporting structure once they're up to speed.

The project timeline remains unchanged. What's shifting is how we divide responsibilities to support the work more sustainably.

If you have questions or concerns about how this affects your work, let's talk.

blocks.text:
Notice what changed: the opening is more direct, each point has its own paragraph, and the timeline now connects to what it means for the team. Because you told Claude exactly what to improve — clarity and flow — it didn't guess.

Notice what didn't change: your tone, your information, your voice. It still sounds like you wrote it.

Here's a trick that makes every edit sound more like you: give Claude a sample of your own writing first. 

Paste a few paragraphs you're happy with and ask it to match that voice — the rhythm, the word choices, the level of formality. The more it has to work from, the closer the result lands to how you'd actually say it.

blocks.text: Adjusting Tone for Different Audiences

Sometimes the structure is fine, but the tone doesn't suit the audience.

You've written a project update for your manager. It's clear and complete, but it feels too informal for senior leadership. You need the same facts presented more formally but without sounding stiff or mechanical.
Draft Example

Here's your draft: "Hey — quick update on the Q4 rollout. We hit a snag with the vendor integration last week, but the team figured out a workaround. Should be back on track by next Friday. Budget's still good, timeline's tight but doable. Let me know if you need more details." It's conversational and efficient — perfect for your direct manager. But for an executive summary? Too casual.

The technical team implemented an alternative solution, with full resolution anticipated by [specific date]. Current status: - Budget remains within approved allocation - Timeline is compressed but achievable with the current mitigation strategy Please contact me if additional details would be useful for leadership planning. The message remains identical — vendor issue, team solution, timeline, and budget status — but the language now matches executive expectations.

blocks.text: Maintaining Coherence in Long Documents

While short writing is forgiving, long documents aren't.

But with Claude as your proofreader, you shouldn't worry.
Imagine you're finalizing a 20-page research report:

• Section 4 was written two weeks ago
  • Section 9 was finished yesterday
The problem? This could result in some inconsistencies.
For example, some of those inconsistencies are:

• Section 4 calls the framework "stakeholder engagement model." Section 9 calls it "participant involvement framework." Same concept, different terms
  • The conclusion references "three core principles," but you actually outlined four in Section 6
These aren't obvious when you're editing piece by piece — but they weaken the document when someone reads it start to finish.

blocks.exampleResponse: I've reviewed the document. Here are the key consistency issues: Terminology misalignment: Section 4 uses "stakeholder engagement model," but Section 9 refers to it as "participant involvement framework." Recommend standardizing on one term throughout. Tone shifts: Sections 1-4 maintain a formal, analytical tone. Section 7 becomes more conversational. Recommend aligning Section 7 with the established tone. Logical gaps: The conclusion references "three core principles," but the document outlines four. Recommend either revising the conclusion or restructuring the principles section. Would you like me to apply these corrections, or would you prefer to review them first?

blocks.text: Writing That Requires Care

Another important thing: some messages require more than clarity. They require care.

You're writing an email to inform your team that a project they've worked on for months is being postponed indefinitely due to budget cuts. You need to be honest about what's happening, but you don't want it to sound cold or dismissive.
Email Draft

Here's your first draft: "Team, I need to let you know that the Atlas project is being postponed indefinitely due to budget reallocations at the company level. I know this is frustrating since we've been working on it for six months, but the decision came from above, and there's nothing we can do about it right now. We'll reassign everyone to other projects next week. Thanks for your work on this."
The information is there, but something feels off:

• "Nothing we can do" sounds dismissive
  • "Thanks for your work" feels like an afterthought

blocks.text: When You Don't Understand Something

Sometimes you encounter a term you don't fully understand. For example, the stress article keeps mentioning "cortisol dysregulation." You know cortisol is a stress hormone, but what does dysregulation really mean?

blocks.exampleResponse: Cortisol dysregulation means your body's stress response system isn't working as it should — either producing too much cortisol at the wrong times, or not enough when you need it. Obvious example: Waking up exhausted despite 8 hours of sleep. Your cortisol should spike in the morning to help you wake up. If it doesn't, you feel groggy all day, even with adequate sleep. Subtle example: Getting a second wind of energy at 10 PM when you're trying to sleep. Your cortisol should drop in the evening. If it spikes instead, your body thinks it's morning and won't let you rest.

Each tool played its role.

The honest up-to-date picture of how tools fit together:
  • Search engines: when you want to browse and judge sources yourself
  • A second AI model (ChatGPT, Gemini): a fast, independent take — useful as a check precisely because it isn't anchored to your Claude conversation
  • Claude: searching, deep understanding, strategic evaluation, and careful refinement — often the whole workflow in one place
The skill isn't collecting tools. It's knowing when one is genuinely worth switching to.
